Born in Parker, South Dakota, the youngest of eleven, with a twin sister, Maurine.
An all-state runner and a big-band jazz trumpeter.
He started at South Dakota State College in 1941, then went to Chicago for defence work,
staying with his sister Charlotte and her husband, the musician Walter Bloom.
He went into the Army on 1 April 1943. The Army’s specialized training program sent him to Pratt Institute in Brooklyn,
where he met Muriel Jackson; when it closed he went to the infantry, by his own account first the 75th Division and
then the 26th Infantry of the First Division, where he served as a private first class.
The family remembered him as captured at the Battle of the Bulge, but the Army's prisoner-of-war records report him
captured on 29 November 1944, in the fighting at the edge of the Hürtgen Forest three weeks before the Bulge began.
He was held at Stalag XII-A at Limburg and then Stalag IX-B, and was freed in the spring of 1945;
that June the Chicago Tribune listed him among liberated prisoners passing through Camp Shanks,
New York. He was discharged on 21 December 1945; the family says he received the Purple Heart.
He played trumpet in Walter Bloom’s touring dance band across the Midwest, went back to college on the GI Bill in
1946, and took a master’s in public administration at NYU in 1949.
He married Muriel in January 1950 and made his life in Connecticut with her: on the research staff of the Connecticut
Public Expenditure Council in Hartford in 1958, and later assistant budget director in the State of Connecticut's
Budget Division, until 1972. Looking back, he wrote that he had been content to “stop and smell the roses” rather
than chase fame and fortune. Born in Hoboken, New Jersey; grew up in Bay Ridge,
Brooklyn. She met Maurice Wintrode during the war, while the Army had him at Pratt Institute in Brooklyn,
and married him in 1950 (the licence ran in the Brooklyn Eagle that January) and raised four children in Connecticut.
